metadata.title: Null mean curvature flow and outermost MOTS

extraction_notes.note: The proof of Lemma 10 cites Lemma~\ref{kappaexists} (itself) among the a-priori estimates, evidently a typo for Lemma 9 (boundaryforkappa); the self-reference edges are marked mention and an edge from Lemma 9 was added.
Theorem 1 calls $\partial\Omega$ 'outer trapped', while every result it rests on assumes outer untrapped; the \label{main} sits after \end{Theorem} but resolves to Theorem 1.

The introduction previews $(**)$, $(*_\varepsilon)$, $(*_{\hat\varepsilon})$ and the translating-graph property; per one-node-per-repeated-statement only the fuller Section 3 versions are nodes (the numbered intro display (3) is kept as an equation).

$(**)$ is stated as 'describes the evolution' (claim) but serves as the defining equation, typed definition; the C-minimizing sentence both imports a definition and asserts $N_k$ satisfies it, typed external definition.
The monotonicity formula is announced in a bold paragraph and derived in running text with no formal statement; the announcement is the claim and the derivation its prose proof.

Theorems 20, 37 and 39 are argued in running text before they are stated; the proof spans were chosen from the first sentence of the argument to the lead-in sentence, and the proof of Theorem 39 contains Lemma 38 and its proof.
Claims 1-4 in the proof of Lemma 36 are author labels (steps) and also numbered, later-cited inline claims, so each is both a labelled step and a nested Level-1 claim.

The unnumbered labelled displays supbnd and measdef get no own nodes (they stay in Lemma 7 and the measures definition); historical and comparative discussion in Sections 1, 4 and 8.1 is not extracted.

nodes.name: Initial data set
nodes.statement: We consider the evolution of hypersurfaces in an initial data set $(M^{n+1},g,K)$ that arises as a spacelike hypersurface $M^{n+1}$ in a Lorentzian spacetime, $(L^{n+2},h)$, with induced metric $g$ and second fundamental form $K$.
nodes.genus: spacelike hypersurface $M^{n+1}$ in a Lorentzian spacetime, $(L^{n+2},h)$
nodes.statement_short: An initial data set $(M,g,K)$ is a spacelike hypersurface of a Lorentzian spacetime with induced metric $g$ and second fundamental form $K$.

nodes.name: Timelike normal $\vec n$ and hypersurface $\Sigma$ with outer normal $\nu$
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{n}$ denote the future directed timelike unit normal vector field of $M\subset L$, and consider a 2-sided closed and bounded hypersurface $\Sigma^{n}\subset M^{n+1}$ with globally defined outer unit normal vector field $\nu$ in $M$.

nodes.name: Null mean curvature flow
nodes.statement: Given a smooth hypersurface immersion $F_{0}:\Sigma\rightarrow M$, the evolution of $\Sigma_{0}:=F_{0}(\Sigma)$ by null mean curvature is the one-parameter family of smooth immersions $F:\Sigma\times[0,T)\rightarrow M$ satisfying \[\tag{$*$} \left\lbrace \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial F}{\partial t}(x,t) & = -(H+P)(x,t)\nu(x,t), \quad x\in\Sigma,\quad t\geq0, \\ F(x,0) & = F_{0}(x),\quad x\in\Sigma{}, \end{aligned} \right. \] where $H:=\text{div}_{\Sigma_t}(\nu)$ denotes the mean curvature of $\Sigma_t:=F(\Sigma,t)$ in $M$ and $P:=\text{tr}_{\Sigma_t}K$ is the trace of $K$ over the tangent space of $\Sigma_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Null mean curvature flow $(*)$: hypersurfaces move inward with normal speed $H+P$, $H$ the mean curvature and $P=\mathrm{tr}_{\Sigma_t}K$.

nodes.name: Null expansion (null mean curvature)
nodes.statement: The quantity $H+P$ corresponds to the {\it null expansion} or \textit{null mean curvature} $\theta_{\Sigma_t}^+$ of $\Sigma_t$ with respect to its future directed outward null vector field $l^+:=\nu+\vec{n}$, \begin{equation*} \theta^+_{\Sigma_t}:=\langle\vec{H}_{\Sigma_t},l^+\rangle_h=H+P, \end{equation*} where $\vec{H}_{\Sigma_t}$, the mean curvature vector of $\Sigma_t$ inside the spacetime $L$, is given by \begin{equation*}\vec{H}_{\Sigma_t}:=H\nu-P\vec{n}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The null expansion $\theta^+=H+P$ is the spacetime mean curvature vector paired with the outward null normal $l^+=\nu+\vec n$.

nodes.name: Initial hypersurface is outer untrapped
nodes.statement: We will also assume that $(H+P)|_{_{\Sigma_0}}>0$ so that the hypersurface $\Sigma_{t}$ contracts under the flow.

nodes.name: Mean curvature flow as time-symmetric special case
nodes.statement: It is a generalization of mean curvature flow in that the latter corresponds to the special time-symmetric case of $(*)$, where $K\equiv0$.

nodes.name: Marginally outer trapped hypersurface (MOTS)
nodes.statement: If $\theta_{\Sigma}^+$ vanishes on all of $\Sigma$, then $\Sigma$ is called a \textit{marginally outer trapped hypersurface}, or MOTS for short.

nodes.name: Schoen-Yau blow-up of Jang's equation
nodes.statement: In their analysis, Schoen and Yau showed that the boundary of the blow-up set of Jang's equation consists of marginally trapped hypersurfaces.
conclusions: the boundary of the blow-up set of Jang's equation consists of marginally trapped hypersurfaces

nodes.name: Existence of MOTS between trapped and untrapped boundaries
nodes.statement: Building upon this work, existence of MOTS in compact data sets with two boundary components, such that the inner boundary is (outer) trapped and the outer boundary is (outer) untrapped, was pointed out by Schoen \cite{S04}, with proofs given by Andersson and Metzger \cite{AM09}, and subsequently by Eichmair \cite{E09} using a different approach.
assumptions: compact data sets with two boundary components, such that the inner boundary is (outer) trapped and the outer boundary is (outer) untrapped

nodes.name: Weak inverse null mean curvature flow jumps to a MOTS
nodes.statement: Jang's equation also featured in the second author's study of weak solutions to the evolution by inverse null mean curvature flow \cite{KM13}, where it was proven that the weak solution starting from any outer trapped initial hypersurface $\partial\Omega_0$ will instantly jump to a MOTS in $M\setminus\bar{\Omega}_0$.

nodes.name: White's outermost minimal hypersurface limit of mean curvature flow
nodes.statement: White \cite{W00} showed that if the initial hypersurface encloses a minimal hypersurface, the outermost such minimal hypersurface will be the stable limit of mean curvature flow.
assumptions: the initial hypersurface encloses a minimal hypersurface
conclusions: the outermost such minimal hypersurface will be the stable limit of mean curvature flow

nodes.name: Level-set formulation
nodes.statement: To develop the weak formulation for the classical evolution $(*$), we use the level-set method and assume the evolving hypersurfaces are given by the level sets, \begin{equation} \Sigma_{t}= \partial\{ x\in M \,\, \big| \,\, u(x)>t \}, \end{equation} of a scalar function $u:M\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: The evolving hypersurfaces are taken to be boundaries of superlevel sets $\{u>t\}$ of a scalar function $u$.

nodes.name: Level sets of $u$
nodes.statement: \Sigma_{t}= \partial\{ x\in M \,\, \big| \,\, u(x)>t \},
nodes.label: levelset1

nodes.name: Downward translating graph (introduction)
nodes.statement: \widetilde\Sigma^{\varepsilon}_t:=\mathrm{graph}\Bigl(\dfrac{u_{\varepsilon}}{\varepsilon}-\frac{t}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)
nodes.label: translating

nodes.name: Main theorem: null mean curvature flow and the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: Let $(M^{n+1},g,K)$ be an initial data set for a space-time, and let $\partial\Omega_{\text{out}}=\Sigma_{\text{out}}$ denote the outermost MOTS in $M$. Let $\Omega$ be a smooth domain in $M$ with $\Omega_\text{out}\subset\Omega$, and whose boundary, $\partial\Omega$, is a mean convex closed and bounded outer trapped embedded hypersurface in $M$. Then for $2\le n\le 6$ the following hold: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item Let $\lambda=\max_i\{|\lambda_i|, \lambda_i\text{ eigenvalue of } K\}$. Then, for any $0<\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda}, \frac12\right\}$ there exists a solution $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}\in C^\infty(\Omega\setminus\Omega_\text{out})$ of the equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ that is zero on $\partial\Omega$ and blows up to infinity over $\Sigma_\text{out}$, that is $\lim_{x\to x_0}\hat u_\varepsilon(x)=\infty$ for any $x_0\in \Sigma_\text{out}$. \item There exists a sequence of $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon_k}$ as in (i) with $\varepsilon_k\downarrow 0$ such that $u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u$ in $C^0(\Omega_1\cup\partial \Omega)$, where $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega)$ and $\Omega_1\subset \Omega\setminus \Omega_\text{out}$ is such that $\partial\Omega\subset\partial\Omega_1$ and $\partial^* (\Omega\setminus\Omega_1)$ is a {\it generalized} MOTS (see Definition~\ref{weakMOTS} and Remark~\ref{weakrmk}). \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $(M^{n+1},g,K)$ be an initial data set for a space-time
$\partial\Omega_{\text{out}}=\Sigma_{\text{out}}$ denote the outermost MOTS in $M$
$\Omega$ be a smooth domain in $M$ with $\Omega_\text{out}\subset\Omega$, and whose boundary, $\partial\Omega$, is a mean convex closed and bounded outer trapped embedded hypersurface in $M$
$2\le n\le 6$
conclusions: there exists a solution $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}\in C^\infty(\Omega\setminus\Omega_\text{out})$ of the equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ that is zero on $\partial\Omega$ and blows up to infinity over $\Sigma_\text{out}$
nodes.statement_short: For $2\le n\le 6$: the regularized equations have solutions blowing up exactly on the outermost MOTS, and a subsequence converges to a weak solution whose limit is a generalized MOTS.
nodes.label: MOTS

nodes.name: Main theorem part (i): blow-up on the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda=\max_i\{|\lambda_i|, \lambda_i\text{ eigenvalue of } K\}$. Then, for any $0<\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda}, \frac12\right\}$ there exists a solution $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}\in C^\infty(\Omega\setminus\Omega_\text{out})$ of the equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ that is zero on $\partial\Omega$ and blows up to infinity over $\Sigma_\text{out}$, that is $\lim_{x\to x_0}\hat u_\varepsilon(x)=\infty$ for any $x_0\in \Sigma_\text{out}$.
assumptions: $0<\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda}, \frac12\right\}$
conclusions: there exists a solution $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}\in C^\infty(\Omega\setminus\Omega_\text{out})$ of the equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ that is zero on $\partial\Omega$ and blows up to infinity over $\Sigma_\text{out}$

nodes.name: Main theorem part (ii): weak limit with generalized MOTS boundary
nodes.statement: There exists a sequence of $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon_k}$ as in (i) with $\varepsilon_k\downarrow 0$ such that $u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u$ in $C^0(\Omega_1\cup\partial \Omega)$, where $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega)$ and $\Omega_1\subset \Omega\setminus \Omega_\text{out}$ is such that $\partial\Omega\subset\partial\Omega_1$ and $\partial^* (\Omega\setminus\Omega_1)$ is a {\it generalized} MOTS (see Definition~\ref{weakMOTS} and Remark~\ref{weakrmk}).

nodes.name: Weak solutions of $(**)$ and $(*)$; outermost MOTS is a boundary
nodes.statement: We will call a function $u$ as in (ii) of Theorem~\ref{MOTS} a weak solution of $(**)$ and its level sets $(\Sigma_t=\{u=t\})_{t\ge 0}$ a weak solution of $(*)$ (see Definition~\ref{weak}). Theorem~\ref{MOTS} (ii) then states that there exists a weak solution of $(*)$ with initial condition $\Sigma_0=\partial\Omega$, $(\Sigma_t)_{t\ge 0}$, that converges to a generalized MOTS that lies outside the outermost MOTS. Note also that the fact that the outermost MOTS has the form $\Sigma_\infty=\partial\Omega_\infty$, where $\Omega_\infty$ is an open set, is not an assumption---this is always the case with $\Omega_\infty$ being the union of all weakly outer trapped sets in $M$, that is open sets with weakly outer trapped boundary (i.e. satisfying $\theta^+\le 0$), as is shown in \cite{AM09}.
nodes.statement_short: Calls $u$ of Theorem 1(ii) a weak solution of $(**)$ (its level sets weakly solve $(*)$); the outermost MOTS bounds the union of weakly outer trapped sets.
nodes.label: thmrmk

nodes.name: Main theorem when the outermost MOTS is empty
nodes.statement: In case $\partial \Omega_\text{out}=\emptyset$, then Theorem~\ref{MOTS} still holds with the functions $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$, as in (i), being defined over all of $\Omega$ (see Theorem \ref{kto0} (iii)).

nodes.name: Generalized MOTS
nodes.statement:
Let $E\subset M$ be a finite perimeter set. We will say that the reduced boundary of $E$, $\partial^*E$, is a generalized MOTS if the following hold  egin{itemize} \item $\mu_E=\mathcal{H}^n\hbox{ {\vrule height .25cm}{\leaders\hrule\hskip.2cm}}\hskip5.0\mu\partial^*E$ carries a generalized mean curvature vector $\vec H$ and \item For $\mathcal{H}^n$-a.e. point on $\partial^*E$ \[\vec H+ P
u=0\,,\,\,	ext{where }P=
u^i
u^jK_{ij}\] and $
u$ is the measure theoretic outer pointing unit normal to $\partial^*E$. \end{itemize} (See \cite[Definition 16.5 and \S14]{LSgmt} for precise definitions of $\partial^*E$, $\vec H$ and $
u$).
differentia: carries a generalized mean curvature vector $\vec H$
nodes.statement_short: $\partial^*E$ is a generalized MOTS if it carries a generalized mean curvature $\vec H$ with $\vec H+P\nu=0$ a.e.
nodes.label: weakMOTS

nodes.name: Regularity of generalized MOTS away from a null set
nodes.statement: If $\partial^* E$ is a generalized MOTS, then by Allard's regularity theorem \cite{Al} (see also \cite{Alex}) we infer that, away from a set of $\mathcal{H}^n$-measure zero, $\partial^*E$ is a $C^{1,\alpha}$ hypersurface for any $\alpha\in (0,1)$. This implies that locally (away from a set of $\mathcal{H}^n$-measure zero) it is the graph of a function that satisfies equation \eqref{Jang} weakly, and using standard PDE methods we obtain that $\partial^* E$ is smooth, and thus a MOTS in the classical sense, away from a set of $\mathcal{H}^n$-measure zero. Furthermore, since the mean curvature is bounded on the reduced boundary, we also have that if $\partial^* E$ is a generalized MOTS then $\mathcal{H}^n(\partial E\setminus\partial^*E)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: By Allard regularity a generalized MOTS is smooth, hence a classical MOTS, off an $\mathcal H^n$-null set, and $\mathcal H^n(\partial E\setminus\partial^*E)=0$.
nodes.label: weakrmk

nodes.name: Where the main theorem is proved
nodes.statement: The proof of the main theorem, Theorem~\ref{main}, is given in Theorems \ref{kto0}, \ref{blowup}, \ref{weak existence} and \ref{MOTSconv}. In Section \ref{properties}, we give various properties for the graphs of the functions $\hat u_\varepsilon$, $\hat u$, the most important being a minimizing property (see Lemmas \ref{emin}, \ref{eminu}). Furthermore, in addition to (locally) uniform convergence of the functions $\hat u_\varepsilon$ to $\hat u$, we obtain convergence, in the sense of varifolds, of their graphs (see Theorem~\ref{mainconvii}).

nodes.name: Weak solutions converge to the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: We believe that weak solutions $(\Sigma_t)_{t\ge0}$ (as in Remark~\ref{thmrmk}) actually converge to the outermost MOTS.

nodes.name: Regular generalized limit equals the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: If the generalized limit can be shown to be regular, then, as it lies outside the outermost MOTS, the two must coincide.
assumptions: the generalized limit can be shown to be regular

nodes.name: Better minimization property of level sets
nodes.statement: We believe that it should be possible to adapt techniques from \cite{W00} to show that the level sets $\Sigma_t$ have a better minimization property (than the one-sided minimization property of Lemma~\ref{eminu}) and thus obtain better regularity for the limit.

nodes.name: Null mean curvature flow via the Laplace-Beltrami operator
nodes.statement: Direct calculation reveals that the null mean curvature flow $(*)$ can be expressed in terms of the Laplace-Beltrami operator $\Delta_{g(t)}$ with respect to the metric $g(t)$ as follows \begin{equation*} \frac{\partial F}{\partial t}(x,t) = \Delta_{g(t)}F(x,t)-g(t)^{ij}K_{ij}.\\ \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Null mean curvature flow is quasi-linear weakly parabolic
nodes.statement: Null mean curvature flow is therefore a quasi-linear, weakly parabolic system which inherits many properties from and indeed formally resembles the standard heat equation (plus a lower order term).

nodes.name: Steepest descent of area plus bulk energy
nodes.statement: It arises as the steepest descent flow of area plus bulk energy $P$, since \begin{equation*} \frac{d}{dt}\left(|\Sigma_t|+\int_{V_t}P dV\right)=-\int_{\Sigma_t} H(H+P) + P(H+P)d\mu=-\int_{\Sigma_t} (H+P)^2 d\mu, \end{equation*} where $V_t$ denotes the volume traced out by the family of hypersurfaces over the time period $[0,t]$.
nodes.statement_short: Along the flow, area plus bulk energy $\int_{V_t}P$ decreases at rate $\int(H+P)^2$.

nodes.name: Evolution equation of the null mean curvature
nodes.label: heH+P

nodes.name: Finite-time singularities for closed initial data
nodes.statement: If, for example, $\Sigma_0$ is closed, the cubic reaction term on the right-hand side guarantees singularity formation in finite time, analogous to the situation for mean curvature flow.

nodes.name: Monotonicity formula for null mean curvature flow
nodes.statement: We do not study the classification of singularities of the evolution by null mean curvature in this paper, however it is interesting to point out that the heat kernel monotonicity formula for mean curvature flow, proven by Huisken in \cite{Hu90}, generalizes to the null mean curvature flow.
nodes.statement_short: Huisken's heat-kernel monotonicity formula extends to null mean curvature flow.

nodes.statement_short: Bound $-Q(\psi)$ by Hamilton's Harnack-type estimate.

nodes.name: Logarithmic inequality
nodes.statement: Using the inequality $x(1+\log(y/x))\le 1+x\log y$ (see \cite{Ha1}) we obtain $-Q(\psi)\le C(1+\psi\log (B(T-t)^{-\frac{n+1}{2}})$ and thus \[\begin{split} \frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Sigma_t}\phi\,d\mu_t &\le\frac{P_0^2}{2}\int_{\Sigma_t}\phi\,d\mu_t + C\log \left(\frac{B}{(T-t)^{\frac{n+1}{2}}}\right)\int_{\Sigma_t}\phi\,d\mu_t\\ &\quad+C(4\pi (T-t))^\frac12|\Sigma_t|. \end{split}\]
nodes.statement_short: Apply $x(1+\log(y/x))\le 1+x\log y$ to get a linear differential inequality.

nodes.name: Integrating factor
nodes.statement: Seting \[\zeta(t)=(T-t)\left(\frac{P_0^2}{2}+C\frac{n+1}{2}+C\log \left(\frac{B}{(T-t)^{\frac{n+1}{2}}}\right)\right), \] we observe that \[\frac{d\zeta}{dt}=-\frac{P_0^2}{2}-C\log \left(\frac{B}{(T-t)^{\frac{n+1}{2}}}\right)\] and thus, \[\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{\zeta(t)}\int\phi d\mu_t\right)\le C(4\pi (T-t))^\frac12|\Sigma_t|.\]
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $e^{\zeta(t)}$ to obtain the monotonicity inequality.

nodes.name: Level-set setting: initial domain mean convex and outer untrapped
nodes.statement: Assume that the evolving hypersurfaces are given by the level sets of a scalar function $u:M\to\mathbb{R}$ via \begin{equation*} E_t:=\{x:u(x)>t\},\quad\quad\Sigma_t:=\partial E_t, \end{equation*} where $E_0=\Omega$ and $\partial \Omega$ is an outer untrapped closed and bounded mean convex hypersurface, so that $(H+P)|_{\partial \Omega}>0$ and $H_{\partial \Omega}>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Superlevel sets $E_t=\{u>t\}$ with $E_0=\Omega$, whose boundary is outer untrapped and mean convex.

nodes.name: Supremum estimate

nodes.name: Proof of the supremum estimate
nodes.statement: Since $\hat u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, either $\hat{u}\leq0$ or $\hat{u}$ has an interior maximum. nodes.statement_short: Maximum principle: evaluate the equation at an interior maximum and use that zero is a subsolution.

nodes.name: Interior maximum bound

nodes.name: Zero is a subsolution

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Serrin's barrier construction [GT, Theorem 14.6].

nodes.name: Level-set form of the operator
nodes.statement:
Since equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa,s})$ is expressed in terms of the geometry of $\mathrm{graph}\hat{u}$, in order to utilize the outer untrapped condition of the boundary $\partial\Omega$, we re-write it instead in terms of the geometry of the individual level sets of $\hat{u}$. To this end, we multiply $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa,s})$ by $v^3=\sqrt{1+|
abla\hat{u}|^2}^3$ to obtain  egin{align*} Q(\hat{u}):=& (1+|
abla\hat{u}|^2)\left(g^{ij}-\dfrac{
abla^i\hat{u}
abla^j\hat{u}}{|
abla \hat{u}|^2+1}ight)
abla_{ij}\hat{u}\ &-s\sqrt{1+|
abla\hat{u}|^2}^3\left(g^{ij}-\dfrac{
abla^i\hat{u}
abla^j\hat{u}}{|
abla \hat{u}|^2+1}ight)K_{ij}\ &+ rac{s}{\varepsilon}(1+|
abla \hat{u}|^2)-\kappa\hat{u}\sqrt{1+|
abla \hat{u}|^2}^3, \end{align*} and decompose it, as in \cite[(14.43)]{GT01}, into the following coefficients  egin{align} Q\hat u&=(\Lambda a^{ij}_{\infty}+a^{ij}_0)
abla_{ij}\hat{u}+|
abla\hat{u}|\Lambda b_{\infty}+b_0=0, \end{align} where \[a^{ij}_{\infty}(x,z,p)=a^{ij}_{\infty}\left(x, rac{p}{|p|}ight)=\left(g^{ij}- rac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2}ight),\,\,a^{ij}_0= rac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2},\,\,\Lambda=1+|p|^2,\] \[b_{\infty}(x,z,p)=b_{\infty}\left(x,z, rac{p}{|p|}ight)=-sK_{ij}\left(g^{ij}- rac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2}ight)-\kappa z\] and \[b_0=-\kappa z rac{\Lambda}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}-sK_{ij}\left(g^{ij} rac{\Lambda}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}+ rac{p^ip^j}{|p|} rac{\Lambda^{1/2}}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}ight)+ rac{s}{\varepsilon}\Lambda.\]
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $v^3$ and decompose the operator into level-set coefficients.

nodes.name: Principal part is level-set null mean curvature
nodes.statement_short: The leading part equals $-(H+sP)-\kappa\hat u$ for the level sets.

nodes.name: Verify structure and boundary conditions
nodes.statement: We see that $b_{\infty}$ is non-increasing in $z$, and also that the correction terms $a_0$ and $b_0$, that arise when considering the curvature of the level sets instead of the graph, are of the order required by the structure condition (14.50) (see also (14.59)) of \cite[Theorem 14.6]{GT01}. That is, $a_0^{ij}=o(\Lambda)$ and $b_0=o(|p|\Lambda)$ as $|p|\to\infty$. Furthermore, since $\partial \Omega$ is outer untrapped, we see that the boundary curvature condition (14.51) of \cite[Theorem 14.6]{GT01} is also satisfied since $H-b_{\infty}=H+sP> 0$ at all points on the boundary $\partial\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Check the structure conditions (14.50) and boundary curvature condition (14.51).

nodes.name: Apply Gilbarg-Trudinger Theorem 14.6
nodes.statement: \cite[Theorem 14.6]{GT01} can then be applied, which implies the existence of an upper barrier at any boundary point, and which depends on the mean curvature of the boundary, $K$ and the supremum bound of of $\hat{u}$ (given in Lemma~\ref{supest}). This finishes the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Apply [GT, Theorem 14.6] to get an upper barrier using the supremum bound.

nodes.name: Existence for $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa,s})$
nodes.statement: Let $(M^{n+1},g,K)$ be an initial data set, $\lambda=\max_i\{|\lambda_i|, \lambda_i\text{ eigenvalue of } K\}$ and $\partial\Omega$ a smooth, strictly mean convex and outer untrapped hypersurface in $M$. Then, for any $\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda},\frac12\right\}$, $\kappa>0$, $s\in[0,1]$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ there exists a solution $\hat{u}\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})$ of $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa,s})$.
assumptions: $(M^{n+1},g,K)$ be an initial data set
$\partial\Omega$ a smooth, strictly mean convex and outer untrapped hypersurface in $M$
$\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda},\frac12\right\}$, $\kappa>0$, $s\in[0,1]$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$
conclusions: there exists a solution $\hat{u}\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})$ of $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa,s})$
nodes.label: kappaexists

nodes.name: Proof of existence for the capillarity problem
nodes.statement_short: Method of continuity in $s$ following Schoen-Yau: closedness from the a-priori estimates and Arzela-Ascoli, openness from the inverse function theorem.

nodes.name: Follow Schoen-Yau
nodes.statement: The proof follows that of \cite[Lemma 3]{SY81}.
nodes.statement_short: The argument follows [SY81, Lemma 3].

nodes.name: Continuity map
nodes.statement:
The idea is to apply the method of continuity to the equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa,s})$. To this end, fix $\varepsilon\le \min\left\{ rac{1}{(n+1)\lambda}, rac12ight\}$ and $\kappa>0$, and define  egin{align*} F^s(w):=\mathrm{div}\left( rac{
abla w}{\sqrt{|
abla w|^2+1}}ight)&-s\left(g^{ij}-\dfrac{
abla^iw
abla^jw}{|
abla w|^2+1}ight)K_{ij}\ &+\dfrac{s}{\varepsilon \sqrt{|
abla w|^2+1}}-\kappa w. \end{align*} For any $\alpha\in (0,1)$, the map  egin{equation*} F: C^{2,\alpha}_0( ar{\Omega})	imes[0,1]	o C^{\alpha}( ar{\Omega}) \end{equation*} given by $F(w,s):=F^s(w)$ has the solution $F(0,0)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the map $F(w,s)=F^s(w)$ with $F(0,0)=0$.

nodes.name: Open-closed reduction
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be the set of $s$ such that $(*_{\varepsilon,\kappa,s})$ has a solution in $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar{\Omega})$ or equivalently the set of $s$ for which there exists $w\in C^{2,\alpha}_0(\bar{\Omega})$ such that $F(w,s)=0$. Then $0\in I$ and we will show that $I$ is an open and closed subset of $[0,1]$, which implies that $I=[0,1]$, thus proving the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Let $I$ be the set of solvable $s$; it suffices to show $I$ is open and closed.

nodes.name: Closedness
nodes.statement: To show that $I$ is closed one uses the a-priori estimates in Lemmas \ref{supest}, \ref{interiorforkappa} and \ref{kappaexists}, standard PDE estimates (which imply `higher' a-priori estimates for a solution; in particular $C^{2,\alpha}$ for any $\alpha\in (0,1)$) and the Arzela-Ascoli theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Closedness from the a-priori estimates, Schauder theory and Arzela-Ascoli.

nodes.name: Openness
nodes.statement: To show that $I$ is open, one has to linearize $F^s$ at a solution $f_0$ and apply the inverse function theorem for Banach spaces. For the details of these two claims we refer the reader to \cite[Lemmas 2 and 3]{SY81} where the arguments on the fact that $I$ is both open and closed are carried out in detail. We remark that the only difference between our case and \cite[Lemma 3]{SY81} is that one has to add the factor $-\frac{\nabla^i f_0}{\varepsilon(|\nabla f_0|^2+1)^\frac32}$ in the term $B^i$ that appears in the linearization of $F^s$ at a solution $f_0$ (the notation being here as in \cite[Lemma 3]{SY81}).
nodes.statement_short: Openness via linearization and the inverse function theorem, as in [SY81].

nodes.name: Regularized Jang's equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa})$
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\varepsilon$, set $s=1$, and study the graphs $N_\kappa$ of solutions of $(*_{\hat\varepsilon,\kappa})$ as $\kappa\to0$.

nodes.name: Equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa})$
Uniform mean curvature bound for $N_\kappa$
nodes.statement: This equation, along with the bound for $|\kappa \hat u_{\varepsilon,\kappa}|$ provided by Lemma~\ref{supest}, shows that the mean curvature of $N_k$ is uniformly bounded by a constant $C= C(\varepsilon)$ independent of $\kappa$.

nodes.name: $C$-minimizing current / $(C,1)$-minimal set
nodes.statement: In the language of {\it currents} or of {\it finite perimeter sets} (codimension 1), the bound on the mean curvature implies that $N_k$ is a {\it $C$-minimizing current} (see \cite{DS93}) or a {\it $(C, 1)$-minimal set} (see \cite{MaMi}), i.e. that \[\underline{\underline{M}}(N_k)\le \underline{\underline{M}}(N_k+\partial Q)+C\underline{\underline{M}}(Q), \forall (n+1)\text{-current }Q.\]
nodes.statement_short: Bounded mean curvature makes $N_\kappa$ $C$-minimizing: mass at most that of any competitor plus $C$ times the swept volume.

nodes.name: Compactness and regularity of $C$-minimizing currents
nodes.statement: Such currents or finite perimeter sets have been extensively studied in \cite{DS93} and \cite{MaMi}, where, among other things, it is shown that they have compactness and regularity properties similar to those of area minimizing currents. The results in \cite{DS93, MaMi} are stated for currents (or sets) in Euclidean space, but the codimension 1 results (the case which is of interest to us here) extend to general Riemannian ambient manifolds, see \cite{Alex}.

nodes.name: Subsequential convergence of $N_{\kappa_i}$ to a regular $C$-minimizing current
nodes.statement: For a sequence $\kappa_i\to 0$ the sequence $\{N_{\kappa_i}\}_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ has a subsequence which converges (in the sense of currents but also as Radon measures) to a {\it$C$-minimizing current} $N$. Furthermore, in dimensions $n\le 6$, $N$ (and any {\it $C$-minimizing current}) has no singular set, i.e. it is a $C^{1}$ manifold.
conclusions: has a subsequence which converges (in the sense of currents but also as Radon measures) to a {\it$C$-minimizing current} $N$
in dimensions $n\le 6$, $N$ (and any {\it $C$-minimizing current}) has no singular set

nodes.name: $C^{1,\alpha}$ convergence of $N_{\kappa_i}$
nodes.statement: We can now prove that the graphs of the sequence $\{N_{\kappa_i}\}$ have locally uniformly bounded $C^{1,\alpha}$ norm and thus the convergence $N_{\kappa_i}\to N$ is actually a $C^{1,\alpha}$ convergence, for any $\alpha\in (0,1)$.

nodes.name: Proof of $C^{1,\alpha}$ and smooth convergence
nodes.statement: This is the result of a standard application of Allard's regularity theorem \cite{Al} on rescalings of $N_{\kappa_i}$ (see \cite{DS93, MaMi, Alex}). The uniform $C^{1,\alpha}$ estimates and standard PDE theory (since the mean curvature of $N_{\kappa_i}$ is expressed in terms of $|\nabla u_{\hat \varepsilon,\kappa_i}|$, see \cite{GT01}), imply now that we have locally uniform $C^{\infty}$ estimates for the graphs $N_{\kappa_i}$ and, as a consequence, the convergence $N_{\kappa_i}\to N$ is smooth.
nodes.statement_short: Allard's regularity theorem on rescalings, then standard elliptic theory upgrades to smooth convergence.

nodes.name: Components of the limit $N$ are embedded graphs
nodes.statement: We now claim that, as a consequence of the Hopf maximum principle, the components of the limit $N$ are embedded graphs.

nodes.name: Limit $\kappa\to0$: blow-up on MOTS
nodes.statement: Assume that $2\le n\le 6$ and let $(M^{n+1},g,K)$ be an initial data set and let $\partial\Omega$ be a smooth, strictly mean convex and outer untrapped hypersurface in $M$. Then, for $\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda},\frac12\right\}$, where $\lambda=\max_i\{|\lambda_i|, \lambda_i\text{ eigenvalue of } K\}$, there exists a sequence $\{\kappa_i\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ with $\kappa_i\downarrow0$, together with an open and connected set $\Omega_\varepsilon$ such that if $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\kappa_i}$ solves $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa_i})$ the following hold. $(i)$ The sequence $\{\hat{u}_{\varepsilon, \kappa_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges uniformly to $+\infty$ on $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon\setminus \partial \Omega$, and $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\kappa_i}$ converges locally smoothly to $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$ in $\Omega_\varepsilon$, where $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$ is a smooth function that satisfies $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ in ${\Omega}_\varepsilon$. $(ii)$ Each boundary component $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$ of $\partial \Omega_\varepsilon\setminus\partial\Omega$ is an embedded MOTS satisfying $\theta^+_{\Sigma_\varepsilon}=H_{\Sigma_{\varepsilon}}+{\mathrm{tr}}_{\Sigma_{\varepsilon}}K=0$, where $H_{\Sigma_{\varepsilon}}$ is the mean curvature of $\Sigma_\varepsilon$ taken with respect to the inward pointing unit normal to $\Omega_\varepsilon$. $(iii)$ If $\Omega$ does not contain a closed MOTS in its interior, $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\kappa_i}$ converges to a smooth solution $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$ of $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ defined on all of $\bar{\Omega}$.
assumptions: $2\le n\le 6$
$(M^{n+1},g,K)$ be an initial data set
$\partial\Omega$ be a smooth, strictly mean convex and outer untrapped hypersurface in $M$
$\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda},\frac12\right\}$
conclusions: The sequence $\{\hat{u}_{\varepsilon, \kappa_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges uniformly to $+\infty$ on $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon\setminus \partial \Omega$
Each boundary component $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$ of $\partial \Omega_\varepsilon\setminus\partial\Omega$ is an embedded MOTS

If $\Omega$ does not contain a closed MOTS in its interior, $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\kappa_i}$ converges to a smooth solution $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$ of $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ defined on all of $\bar{\Omega}$.
nodes.statement_short: As $\kappa_i\to0$, solutions converge to a solution of $(*_{\hat\varepsilon})$ on $\Omega_\varepsilon$ that blows up exactly on a MOTS.
nodes.label: kto0

nodes.name: Proof of the $\kappa\to0$ blow-up theorem
nodes.statement:
As we explained before the statement of the theorem, using standard results of $(C,1)$-minimal sets (see \cite{MaMi}), we have that the graphs $N_{\kappa_ i}$ of the functions $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\kappa_i}$ converge locally smoothly to a smooth embedded hypersurface $N$ in $ ar{\Omega}	imes\mathbb{R}$. Moreover, since $N$ inherits its orientation from $N_{\kappa_i}$, it follows that $ rac{1}{v_{\kappa_i}}=(\sqrt{1+|
abla\hat{u}_{\varepsilon, \kappa_i}|^2})^{-1}$ converges (smoothly) to the vertical component, $ rac{1}{v}$, of the unit normal vector of $N$. In view of \eqref{Harnack}, this limit satisfies $\Delta^N\left( rac{1}{v}ight)+ rac{1}{\varepsilon} ar g\left(

Furthermore, the boundary gradient estimates given in Lemma~ef{boundaryforkappa} ensures that the graphs $N_{\kappa_i}$ must remain bounded near $\partial\Omega$, and thus the limit $N$ is a graph near $\partial\Omega$. Therefore, $N$ is the graph of a function, which we call $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$, defined on an open (non-empty) subset of $\Omega$, which we call $\Omega_\varepsilon$. The locally smooth convergence $\hat u_{\varepsilon, \kappa_i}	o\hat u_\varepsilon$ then immediately yields that $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$ satisfies $(*_{\hat\varepsilon})$ in ${\Omega}_\varepsilon$ and diverges to infinity on approach to $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon\setminus\partial\Omega$. This finishes the proof of (i). To prove (ii), we need to show that the set $\Sigma_\varepsilon=\partial\Omega_\varepsilon\setminus \partial \Omega$, where the function $\hat u_\varepsilon$ tends to infinity, is a MOTS (note $\Sigma_\varepsilon$ as defined here might have more than one connected component). Since $N=\mathrm{graph} \hat u_\varepsilon$ over $\Omega_\varepsilon$ and $\hat u_\varepsilon$ satisfies $(*_{\hat\varepsilon})$, we have that $H+P= rac{1}{\varepsilon\sqrt{1+|

u(x)$ is the upward pointing unit normal to $N$ at $(x, \hat u_\varepsilon(x))$ and $
u^{n+2}$ is its vertical component. We consider vertical translations, $N_{\alpha_i}= N-\alpha_i$, of $N$ for a sequence $\{\alpha_i\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\subset \mathbb{R}$ with $a_i\uparrow \infty$. $N_{\alpha_i}$ have uniformly bounded mean curvature and thus are $(C,1)$-minimal sets. Therefore, we can argue as with the convergence $N_{\kappa_ i}	o N$, using the results of \cite{DS93, MaMi}, to conclude that, after passing to a subsequence, $N_{\alpha_i}	o \widetilde N$ locally smoothly (note again that the mean curvature of $N_{\alpha_i}$ can be expressed in terms of its normal). Since we also have that $N_{\alpha_i}	o \Sigma_\varepsilon	imes \mathbb{R}$ locally uniformly, we conclude that $\widetilde N =\Sigma_\varepsilon	imes \mathbb{R}$. nodes.name: Proof of (i)
nodes.statement: As we explained before the statement of the theorem, using standard results of $(C,1)$-minimal sets (see \cite{MaMi}), we have that the graphs $N_{\kappa_ i}$ of the functions $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\kappa_i}$ converge locally smoothly to a smooth embedded hypersurface $N$ in $\bar{\Omega}\times\mathbb{R}$. Moreover, since $N$ inherits its orientation from $N_{\kappa_i}$, it follows that $\frac{1}{v_{\kappa_i}}=(\sqrt{1+|\nabla\hat{u}_{\varepsilon, \kappa_i}|^2})^{-1}$ converges (smoothly) to the vertical component, $\frac{1}{v}$, of the unit normal vector of $N$. In view of \eqref{Harnack}, this limit satisfies $\Delta^N\left(\frac{1}{v}\right)+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\bar g\left(\nabla^N \frac{1}{v},\tau\right)-\frac{\beta}{v}\leq0$. The Hopf maximum principle then says that on each connected component of $N$, we have that $\frac{1}{v}$ either vanishes identically---and the connected component is cylindrical---or else is everywhere positive---and the connected component is a graph. Furthermore, the boundary gradient estimates given in Lemma~\ref{boundaryforkappa} ensures that the graphs $N_{\kappa_i}$ must remain bounded near $\partial\Omega$, and thus the limit $N$ is a graph near $\partial\Omega$. nodes.name: Vertical translations converge
nodes.statement: We consider vertical translations, $N_{\alpha_i}= N-\alpha_i$, of $N$ for a sequence $\{\alpha_i\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\subset \mathbb{R}$ with $a_i\uparrow \infty$. $N_{\alpha_i}$ have uniformly bounded mean curvature and thus are $(C,1)$-minimal sets. Therefore, we can argue as with the convergence $N_{\kappa_ i}\to N$, using the results of \cite{DS93, MaMi}, to conclude that, after passing to a subsequence, $N_{\alpha_i}\to \widetilde N$ locally smoothly (note again that the mean curvature of $N_{\alpha_i}$ can be expressed in terms of its normal).
nodes.statement_short: Translates $N-\alpha_i$ are $(C,1)$-minimal and converge smoothly to some $\widetilde N$.

nodes.name: Limit cylinder is a MOTS
nodes.statement: Since we also have that $N_{\alpha_i}\to \Sigma_\varepsilon\times \mathbb{R}$ locally uniformly, we conclude that $\widetilde N =\Sigma_\varepsilon\times \mathbb{R}$. The locally smooth convergence $N_{\alpha_i}\to \Sigma_\varepsilon\times \mathbb{R}$, along with the fact that for $N=\mathrm{graph} \hat u_\varepsilon$ we have $H+P=\frac 1\varepsilon \nu^{n+2}$, implies that the limit $\Sigma_\varepsilon\times \mathbb{R}$ is a MOTS.
nodes.statement_short: $\widetilde N=\Sigma_\varepsilon\times\mathbb R$ and $H+P=\nu^{n+2}/\varepsilon\to0$ there.

nodes.name: Proof of (iii)
nodes.statement: Finally, we note that if $\Omega$ does not contain a closed MOTS in its interior, then $\Sigma_\varepsilon=\emptyset$ and therefore (iii) holds.
nodes.statement_short: No closed MOTS inside means empty blow-up set.

nodes.name: Elliptic regularization locates MOTS
nodes.statement: It is interesting to observe that the elliptic regularization problem $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ provides a new way to locate MOTS in space-time initial data sets with a mean convex, outer-untrapped hypersurface. In the following section we will show that the hypersufaces $\Sigma_\varepsilon$ are not only MOTS but they are indeed the outermost MOTS and thus this is actually a way to locate the outermost MOTS.

nodes.name: Stability of the outermost MOTS and trapped surfaces inside it
nodes.statement: It is known that the outermost MOTS, $\Sigma_\text{out}=\partial \Omega_\text{out}$, is stable (see \cite{AM09}), something that was used in the proof of \cite[Theorem 5.1]{AM09} to show that one can change the initial data $K$ in $\Omega_\text{out}$, so that there exists a smooth outer trapped hypersurface $\Sigma^-$ (i.e. satisfying $\theta^+(\Sigma^-)=H+P<0$) inside $\Sigma_\text{out}$ (i.e. $\Sigma^-\subset\Omega_\text{out}$).

nodes.name: Claim: a suitable $\psi$ suffices
nodes.statement: We claim now that there exists a $C^2$ function $\psi:[0,\tau]\to \mathbb{R}$ such that $v=\psi\circ u\in C^2(U)$ and such that \[v(x)=\psi(u(x))=\begin{cases}\psi(\tau)=0&\text{ on }\partial U,\\ \psi(0)\ge \frac{1}{\delta} &\text{ in } U\setminus U_\tau, \end{cases}\] and \begin{equation} -\psi'-\min\left\{C_0^2|\psi''|,\frac{|\psi''|}{(\psi')^2}\right\}\ge -C=-C(\tau, C_0). \end{equation} The existence of such a function $\psi$ implies then, after using the estimates \eqref{term1}, \eqref{term2} and \eqref{psi'} in \eqref{Mk}, \[ \mathcal M_\varepsilon(v)\ge\frac{1}{\varepsilon}-C_0-C,\] where $C=C(\tau, C_0)$ is the constant from the estimate \eqref{psi'}, and thus taking $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_1(C_0,\tau)=({C_0+C})^{-1}$ we have that for all $\varepsilon\le \varepsilon_1$ \[\mathcal M_\varepsilon(v)\ge 0.\] This concludes the proof of the lemma, provided that there exists a function $\psi$ as we claimed above and which we now construct.
nodes.statement_short: If $\psi$ satisfies (31), then $\mathcal M_\varepsilon(v)\ge 1/\varepsilon-C_0-C\ge0$ for $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_1$; it remains to construct $\psi$.

nodes.name: Profile function $\zeta$
nodes.statement: For any $\delta\in(0,1]$, we define $\zeta:[0,2]\to\mathbb{R}$ by \[\zeta(t)=\begin{cases}\log\left(\frac{t}{\delta}+1\right)&\text{ for } t\in\left[0,1\right],\\ c_1+c_0\left(t-1\right)-\frac{c_0^2}{2}\left(t-1\right)^2\\ \hspace{.4cm}+\frac{2c_0^2-3c_0}{3}\left(t-1\right)^3+\frac{-c_0^2+2c_0}{4}\left(t-1\right)^4 &\text{ for } t\in\left[1,2\right], \end{cases}\] where $c_1=\log\left(\frac1\delta+1\right)$ and $c_0=\frac{1}{1+\delta}$. Note first that \[\zeta(t)=\begin{cases}0&\text{ for } t=0,\\ c_1+\frac{c_0}{2}-\frac{c_0^2}{12}\ge c_1=\log\left(\frac1\delta+1\right)&\text{ for } t=2. \end{cases}\] For the derivatives of $\zeta$, we have \[\zeta'(t)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{t+\delta}&\text{ for } t\in\left(0,1\right],\\ \frac{1}{1+\delta}=c_0&\text{ for } t=1,\\ c_0-{c_0^2}\left(t-1\right)+({2c_0^2-3c_0})\left(t-1\right)^2,\\ \hspace{.4cm}+({-c_0^2+2c_0})\left(t-1\right)^3 &\text{ for } t\in\left[1,2\right]\\ 0&\text{ for } t=2, \end{cases}\] and \[\zeta''(t)=\begin{cases}-\frac{1}{(t+\delta)^2}&\text{ for } t\in\left(0,1\right],\\ -\frac{1}{(1+\delta)^2}=-c_0^2&\text{ for } t=1,\\ -{c_0^2}+({4c_0^2-6c_0})\left(t-1\right)+({-3c_0^2+6c_0})\left(t-1\right)^2 &\text{ for } t\in\left[1,2\right],\\ 0&\text{ for } t=2, \end{cases}\] where of course here at $t=2$ we mean the left derivatives, and hence $\zeta$ is a $C^2$ function.
nodes.statement_short: Define the $C^2$ profile $\zeta$ (logarithmic then quartic) and compute its derivatives.

nodes.name: Derivative inequality for $\zeta$
nodes.statement: We further note that \[\zeta'-\min\left\{|\zeta''|,\frac{|\zeta''|}{(\zeta')^2}\right\}\ge\begin{cases}\zeta' -\frac{|\zeta''|}{(\zeta')^2}\ge -1&\text{ for } t\in\left(0,1\right],\\ \zeta'-|\zeta''|\ge -20c_0\ge -20&\text{ for } t\in\left[1,2\right]. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Check $\zeta'-\min\{|\zeta''|,|\zeta''|/(\zeta')^2\}$ is bounded below.

nodes.name: Define $\psi$ by rescaling
nodes.statement: We now define the function $\psi:[0,\tau]\to\mathbb{R}$ by \[\psi(t)=\zeta\left(\frac{2}{\tau}(\tau-t)\right)\] and claim that this is the desired function. Note first that $\psi\in C^2((0,\tau))$ and for the (right) derivatives at zero we have \[\psi'(0)=-\frac{2}{\tau}\zeta'(2)=0\,\,,\,\,\psi''(0)=\frac{4}{\tau^2}\zeta''(2)=0.\] Hence, the function $v=\psi\circ u$ is also $C^2$ and satisfies \[v(x)=\psi(u(x))=\begin{cases}\psi(\tau)=\zeta(0)=0&\text{ on }\partial U,\\ \psi(0)=\zeta(2)\ge c_1=\log\left(\frac1\delta+1\right) &\text{ in } U\setminus U_\tau. \end{cases}\]
nodes.statement_short: Set $\psi(t)=\zeta(2(\tau-t)/\tau)$; $v$ is $C^2$ with the right boundary values.

nodes.name: Verify (31)
nodes.statement: Finally, we have \[\begin{split}-\psi'(t)&-\min\left\{C_0^2|\psi''|,\frac{|\psi''|}{(\psi')^2}\right\}\\ &=\frac{2}{\tau}\zeta'\left(\frac2\tau(\tau-t)\right)-\min\left\{\frac{4 C_0^2}{\tau ^2}|\zeta''|,\frac{|\zeta''|}{(\zeta')^2}\right\} \ge -20\frac{4 C_0^2}{\tau^2}. \end{split}\] Therefore, the function $\psi$ as defined above has all the required properties, after replacing $\delta$ by $(e^{1/\delta}-1)^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\psi$ satisfies (31), completing the construction.

nodes.name: Blow-up exactly on the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: There exists an $\varepsilon_0$ depending only on the initial data, such that for any $\varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$ the following holds. There exists a solution $\hat u_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\Omega_0)$ of the equation ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$), where $\Omega_0=\Omega\setminus\overline\Omega_\infty$, such that $\hat u_\varepsilon$ blows up over the inner boundary $\partial\Omega_0\setminus\partial\Omega=\Sigma_\text{out}$ (the outermost MOTS) and is zero over the outer boundary $\partial \Omega$. Consequently the function $u_\varepsilon=\varepsilon\hat u_\varepsilon$ is then a smooth solution of ($*_{\varepsilon}$) in $\Omega_0$ that blows up over the inner boundary $\Sigma_\text{out}$ (the outermost MOTS) and is zero over the outer boundary $\partial \Omega$.
conclusions: There exists a solution $\hat u_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\Omega_0)$ of the equation ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$), where $\Omega_0=\Omega\setminus\overline\Omega_\infty$, such that $\hat u_\varepsilon$ blows up over the inner boundary $\partial\Omega_0\setminus\partial\Omega=\Sigma_\text{out}$ (the outermost MOTS) and is zero over the outer boundary $\partial \Omega$.
assumptions: for any $\varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$
nodes.statement_short: For small $\varepsilon$, $(*_{\hat\varepsilon})$ has a solution on $\Omega\setminus\overline\Omega_\infty$ blowing up exactly on the outermost MOTS.
nodes.label: blowup

nodes.name: Value of $\varepsilon_0$
nodes.statement: The $\varepsilon_0$ of the theorem is given by $\varepsilon_0=\min\left\{\frac12, \frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda'}, \varepsilon_1\right\}$, where $\lambda'=\max_i\{|\lambda'_i|, \lambda_i\text{ eigenvalue of } K'\}$ and $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_1(C_0,\tau)$, $C_0$ and $\tau$ are as in Lemma~\ref{barrier}. The reason for the dependence of $\varepsilon_0$ on $K'$, instead of $K$, is that we want Theorem~\ref{kto0} to hold with $K$ replaced by the new data $K'$.

nodes.name: Proof of blow-up on the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: We will make use of the new data $K'$ as in \eqref{K'}, which also satisfy \eqref{lK}. Let ($*_{\hat \varepsilon, \kappa}$)' and ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$)' denote the equations ($*_{\hat \varepsilon, \kappa}$) and ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$) after we have replaced $K$ by $K'$. Note first that we can repeat the estimates of Sections \ref{ellregsection} and \ref{eexistencesection} with the new data $K'$ (in the place of $K$) and thus Theorem~\ref{kto0} holds with $K$ replaced by $K'$ and equations ($*_{\hat \varepsilon, \kappa}$) and ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$) replaced by ($*_{\hat \varepsilon, \kappa}$)' and ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$)'. Theorem~\ref{kto0} (i) then implies that for any $\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac12, \frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda'}\right\}$, where $\lambda'=\max_i\{|\lambda'_i|, \lambda_i\text{ eigenvalue of } K'\}$, there exists an open and connected set $\Omega_\varepsilon\subset \Omega$ and a solution $\hat u_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\Omega_\varepsilon)$ of ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$)', with $\hat u_\varepsilon=0$ on $\partial \Omega\subset \partial\Omega_\varepsilon$ and $\hat u_\varepsilon$ blowing up on the other boundary components. Furthermore, by Theorem~\ref{kto0} (ii), we have that $\partial \Omega_\varepsilon\setminus\partial \Omega$ is a MOTS. Let now $\Sigma^-$, $U$, and $v$ be as in Lemma~\ref{barrier} for some $\delta>0$ . Then, for $\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac12, \frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda}, \varepsilon_1\right\}$ (where $\varepsilon_1$ is as in Lemma~\ref{barrier}), by the comparison principle we have that $v\le \hat u_\varepsilon$ over $U$ and thus $\frac{1}{\delta}\le \hat u_\varepsilon$ over $\Sigma^-$. Since this is true for any $\delta>0$ we obtain that the MOTS $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon\setminus \Omega$ must lie outside $\Sigma^-$. Recall now that by the construction of the new data $K'$ (in the beginning of this section) the region between $\Sigma^-$ and the outermost MOTS, $\Sigma_\text{out}$, is foliated by outer trapped hypersurfaces $\Sigma_{out,t}$. The maximum principle then implies that the MOTS $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon\setminus \Omega$ cannot enter the open region between $\Sigma^-$ and the outermost MOTS and therefore it must coincide with the outermost MOTS, $\Sigma_\text{out}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the $\kappa\to0$ theorem with modified data $K'$; the barrier lemma and comparison force the blow-up MOTS outside $\Sigma^-$. The trapped foliation and maximum principle then pin it to $\Sigma_{out}$.

nodes.name: Modified equations
nodes.statement: We will make use of the new data $K'$ as in \eqref{K'}, which also satisfy \eqref{lK}. Let ($*_{\hat \varepsilon, \kappa}$)' and ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$)' denote the equations ($*_{\hat \varepsilon, \kappa}$) and ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$) after we have replaced $K$ by $K'$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $K$ by $K'$ in the equations.

nodes.name: Apply the $\kappa\to0$ theorem to $K'$
nodes.statement: Note first that we can repeat the estimates of Sections \ref{ellregsection} and \ref{eexistencesection} with the new data $K'$ (in the place of $K$) and thus Theorem~\ref{kto0} holds with $K$ replaced by $K'$ and equations ($*_{\hat \varepsilon, \kappa}$) and ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$) replaced by ($*_{\hat \varepsilon, \kappa}$)' and ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$)'. Theorem~\ref{kto0} (i) then implies that for any $\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac12, \frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda'}\right\}$, where $\lambda'=\max_i\{|\lambda'_i|, \lambda_i\text{ eigenvalue of } K'\}$, there exists an open and connected set $\Omega_\varepsilon\subset \Omega$ and a solution $\hat u_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\Omega_\varepsilon)$ of ($*_{\hat\varepsilon}$)', with $\hat u_\varepsilon=0$ on $\partial \Omega\subset \partial\Omega_\varepsilon$ and $\hat u_\varepsilon$ blowing up on the other boundary components. Furthermore, by Theorem~\ref{kto0} (ii), we have that $\partial \Omega_\varepsilon\setminus\partial \Omega$ is a MOTS.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 11 with $K'$ gives $\hat u_\varepsilon$ on $\Omega_\varepsilon$ blowing up on a MOTS.

nodes.name: Barrier comparison
nodes.statement: Let now $\Sigma^-$, $U$, and $v$ be as in Lemma~\ref{barrier} for some $\delta>0$ . Then, for $\varepsilon\le \min\left\{\frac12, \frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda}, \varepsilon_1\right\}$ (where $\varepsilon_1$ is as in Lemma~\ref{barrier}), by the comparison principle we have that $v\le \hat u_\varepsilon$ over $U$ and thus $\frac{1}{\delta}\le \hat u_\varepsilon$ over $\Sigma^-$. Since this is true for any $\delta>0$ we obtain that the MOTS $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon\setminus \Omega$ must lie outside $\Sigma^-$.
nodes.statement_short: Comparison with the barrier $v$ gives $\hat u_\varepsilon\ge1/\delta$ on $\Sigma^-$ for every $\delta$.

nodes.name: Maximum principle pins the MOTS
nodes.statement: Recall now that by the construction of the new data $K'$ (in the beginning of this section) the region between $\Sigma^-$ and the outermost MOTS, $\Sigma_\text{out}$, is foliated by outer trapped hypersurfaces $\Sigma_{out,t}$. The maximum principle then implies that the MOTS $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon\setminus \Omega$ cannot enter the open region between $\Sigma^-$ and the outermost MOTS and therefore it must coincide with the outermost MOTS, $\Sigma_\text{out}$.
nodes.statement_short: The trapped foliation between $\Sigma^-$ and $\Sigma_{out}$ forces the MOTS to be $\Sigma_{out}$.

nodes.name: Uniform gradient estimate
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon\le \frac12$ and $u_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\Omega_0)$ be a solution of $(*_{\varepsilon})$ as in Theorem~\ref{blowup}. Then, $u_\varepsilon$ satisfies the estimate \begin{equation*} \sup_{\Omega_{T/2}}|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\leq \frac{2}{\eta T}\exp(\eta T)\cdot\sup_{\partial\Omega}(1+\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}^2|}), \end{equation*} where $\eta$ is a constant that depends only on the initial data, in fact $\eta=\eta(n,\mathrm{Ric},\|K\|_{C^1})$, and $\Omega_T=\{x\in\bar{\Omega}_0:u_{\varepsilon}(x)\leq T\}$.
assumptions: $\varepsilon\le \frac12$
$u_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\Omega_0)$ be a solution of $(*_{\varepsilon})$ as in Theorem~\ref{blowup}
nodes.statement_short: Interior gradient bound for $u_\varepsilon$ on $\{u_\varepsilon\le T/2\}$, uniform in $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Maximum principle inequality
nodes.statement: At a maximum point $x_0$, where $\Delta((w-w_0)v)\leq0$ and $\nabla((w-w_0)v)=0$, \eqref{newJacobiEqn} reduces to \begin{align*} 0\geq (w-w_0)v\Bigg(&|A|^2+\left(1-\frac{1}{v^2}\right)\mathrm{Ric}(\gamma,\gamma)\\ &+(\varepsilon\eta)^2\left(1-\frac{1}{v^2}\right)+\varepsilon\eta\frac{H}{v}-v\bar g(\nabla^NH,\tau)\Bigg)\\ &+w_0v\left((\varepsilon\eta)^2\left(1-\frac{1}{v^2}\right)+\varepsilon\eta\frac{H}{v}\right). \end{align*} After implementing the above estimates and also using \eqref{floweqn2}, this becomes \begin{align*} 0\geq(w-w_0)v\Bigg(\frac{|A|^2}{2}&+\left(1-\frac{1}{v^2}\right)\Bigl(\mathrm{Ric}(\gamma,\gamma)+\eta+(\varepsilon\eta)^2\Bigr)\\ &\hspace{3cm}+\frac{\eta}{v^2}-\varepsilon\eta\frac{\|K\|_{C^0}}{v}-2c^2\Bigg)\\ &+w_0v\left((\eta+(\varepsilon\eta)^2)\left(1-\frac{1}{v^2}\right)+\frac{\eta}{v^2}-\varepsilon\eta\frac{\|K\|_{C^0}}{v}\right). \end{align*}

nodes.statement: By the contradiction hypothesis (\ref{contradiction}), we find that $v(x_0)>\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ and thus $(1-\frac{1}{v^2})>\frac{1}{2}$, provided that $\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{2}$. nodes.name: Barrier strategy
nodes.statement: The idea of the proof is to create an upper barrier for the functions $u_\varepsilon$ at the boundary $\partial\Omega$, by bending the (short time) smooth solution of $(*)$ with initial data $\partial \Omega$. This construction is similar to that in \cite[Lemma 4.2]{S08} with the extra complication that here we do not have a supremum estimate for the solutions $u_\varepsilon$ (a construction of a barrier using the smooth solution was also used in Lemma~\ref{barrier}).
nodes.statement_short: Build an upper barrier at $\partial\Omega$ by bending the smooth flow.

nodes.name: Arrival time of the smooth flow
nodes.statement:
Let $F(\cdot,t):\partial\Omega	imes[0,T)	o M$ be the unique solution to $(*)$, with initial condition $F(\cdot, 0)=\mathrm{Id}_{\partial\Omega	o\partial\Omega}$ and let $\Sigma_t=F(\partial\Omega, t)$ (see Remark~ef{SUrmk} for the existence of $F$). Since the null mean curvature of the hypersurfaces remains positive (see Remark~ef{SUrmk}), we obtain that $\Sigma _{t_1}\cap \Sigma_{t_2}=\emptyset$ for $t_1
e t_2$. For any $	au\in (0, T)$ we define \[ \Omega_	au= igcup_{0<t<	au}\Sigma_t\subset \Omega, \] and let $u:\Omega_	au	o \mathbb{R}^+$ be defined by $u(p)=t\Leftrightarrow p\in \Sigma_t$. Then, we have that $u$ is a smooth solution of $(**)$ over $\overline\Omega_	au$ and furthermore there exists some constant $C_0>1$ such that  egin{equation}  rac{1}{C_0}\le |
abla u|\le C_0\,\,,\,\,|
abla^2 u|\le C_0	ext{ in }\overline \Omega_	au. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Bending function
nodes.statement: We choose $0<\tau<T$ such that $\tau<\frac{1}{2}$ and bend the smooth solution $u$ of $(**)$ to construct a supersolution of $(*_{\varepsilon})$ that is zero on $\partial\Omega$ and goes to infinity on the inner boundary $\Sigma_{\tau}$ of $\Omega_{\tau}$. To this end, we define $\psi:[0, \tau)\to \mathbb{R}^+$ to be the following smooth increasing function \begin{equation} \psi(t)=2t+\frac{1}{\tau-t}-\frac{1}{\tau}. \end{equation} Then $\psi(0)=0$, $\lim_{t\to\tau}\psi(t)=+\infty$ and furthermore we have \begin{equation} \psi'(t)=2+\frac{1}{(\tau-t)^2}\,\,,\quad \psi''(t)=\frac{2}{(\tau-t)^3}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi(t)=2t+1/(\tau-t)-1/\tau$.

nodes.statement: We will show that the function \[v(x)=\psi(u(x))\] is a super solution of $(*_{\varepsilon})$ in $\Omega_\tau$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. Since $u_{\varepsilon}$ solves $(*_{\varepsilon})$ with $u_\varepsilon=0$ on $\partial \Omega$, this would then imply that $u_{\varepsilon}\leq v$ on $\bar{\Omega}_{\tau}$ and \[ \sup_{\partial \Omega}|\nabla u_\varepsilon|\le \sup_{\partial \Omega}|\nabla v|\le \left(2+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right) C_0,\] which proves the lemma with $C=(2+\tau^{-2})C_0$. Hence, it suffices to show that there exists $\varepsilon_0$, depending only on the initial data, such that $v$ is a super solution of $(*_{\varepsilon})$ for all $\varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$.

nodes.name: Supersolution
nodes.statement: Putting everything together and using these estimates back in \eqref{Mev}, we find that for $\varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$, where $\varepsilon_0=\min\{(4(n+1)\lambda)^{-1}, C_0^{-2}\}$, we obtain the estimate \[\mathcal M_\varepsilon(v) \le 1-\psi' +{1},\] which due to \eqref{Dpsidelta} implies \[ \mathcal M_\varepsilon(v) \le 1-\left(2+\frac{1}{(\tau-t)^2}\right) +{1}\le-\frac{1}{(\tau-t)^2}<0, \] so that $v$ is a super solution and thus $u_\varepsilon\le v$ for all $\varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$.

nodes.name: Construction of the weak solution (limit $\varepsilon\to0$)
nodes.statement_short: The $\varepsilon$-uniform gradient estimates and Arzela-Ascoli give a locally uniform limit $u$; Banach-Alaoglu gives weak convergence of gradients.

nodes.name: Convergence $u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u$
nodes.statement: u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u \text{ in $C^0({\Omega_1}\cup\partial\Omega)$},
nodes.label: uetou

nodes.name: Weak convergence of gradients
nodes.statement: \int_{\Omega_1}\nabla u_{\varepsilon_k}\cdot fd\mathcal{H}^n\to \int_{\Omega_1}\nabla u\cdot fd\mathcal{H}^n\,,\,\,\forall f\in L^1_c(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{n+1}),
nodes.label: Duetou

nodes.name: Arzela-Ascoli
nodes.statement: We now return to the original elliptic regularization problem $(*_{\varepsilon})$, and note that the a-priori estimates for $u_{\varepsilon}$ given in Lemmas \ref{unigradest} and \ref{bdrygradest} are uniform in $\varepsilon$. We can therefore use the Arzela--Ascoli theorem to extract a limit as $\varepsilon\to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform estimates allow extracting a limit by Arzela-Ascoli.

nodes.name: Limit function $u$
nodes.statement: In particular, there exists $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega)$ and a sequence $\varepsilon_k\downarrow 0$ such that \begin{equation} u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u \text{ in $C^0({\Omega_1}\cup\partial\Omega)$}, \end{equation} where $\Omega_1\stackrel{open}{\subset}\Omega_0$ is such that $\partial\Omega_1\supset\partial\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $u$ and $\varepsilon_k\downarrow0$ with $u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u$ on $\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega$.

nodes.name: $\Omega_1$ is nonempty
nodes.statement: In particular, with $\Omega_2=\cap_t\cup _k\{u_{\varepsilon_k}>t\}$, we have $\Omega_1=\Omega_0\setminus\overline\Omega_2$ and thus Lemma~\ref{bdrygradest} implies that $\Omega_1\ne\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Boundary gradient bound shows $\Omega_1\neq\emptyset$.

nodes.name: Blow-up at the inner boundary
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since the functions $u_{\varepsilon_k}$ tend to $+\infty$ on approach to $\partial\Omega_0\setminus\partial\Omega$, the limit function $u$ also tends to $+\infty$ on approach to $\partial\Omega_1\setminus\partial\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: $u\to+\infty$ at $\partial\Omega_1\setminus\partial\Omega$.

nodes.name: Meaning of local convergence
nodes.statement: With the convergence `in $C^0({\Omega_1}\cup\partial\Omega)$' above we mean that $u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u$ uniformly in any compact subset of ${\Omega_1}\cup\partial\Omega$. Similarly with `$u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega)$' we mean that $u$ is Lipschitz in any compact subset of ${\Omega_1}\cup\partial\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Convergence and Lipschitz regularity are meant on compact subsets.

nodes.name: Weak gradient convergence
nodes.statement: Furthermore, Lemma~\ref{unigradest}, along with the Banach--Alaoglu theorem, implies that \begin{equation} \int_{\Omega_1}\nabla u_{\varepsilon_k}\cdot fd\mathcal{H}^n\to \int_{\Omega_1}\nabla u\cdot fd\mathcal{H}^n\,,\,\,\forall f\in L^1_c(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{n+1}), \end{equation} where $L^1_c(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ denotes all the functions in $L^1(\Omega_1;\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ with support in a compact subset of $\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Banach-Alaoglu gives weak convergence of $\nabla u_{\varepsilon_k}$.

nodes.name: Weak solution of $(**)$
nodes.statement: A function $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1)$ defined as the limit of a sequence $\{u_{\varepsilon_k}\}$ of solutions to $(*_{\varepsilon_k})$, with $\varepsilon_k\downarrow 0$, as in \eqref{uetou} will be called a weak solution of $(**)$.
differentia: defined as the limit of a sequence $\{u_{\varepsilon_k}\}$ of solutions to $(*_{\varepsilon_k})$, with $\varepsilon_k\downarrow 0$
nodes.label: weak

nodes.name: Existence of weak solutions
nodes.statement: There exists $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega)$ a weak solution of $(**)$, as in Definition~\ref{weak}, where $\Omega_1\stackrel{open}{\subset} (\Omega\setminus\overline\Omega_\text{out})$ and $\partial\Omega_1\supset\partial\Omega$ (recall that $\Omega_\text{out}$ is such that $\partial\Omega_\text{out}=\Sigma_\text{out}$, the outermost MOTS). Furthermore, any weak solution satisfies $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ and $\lim_{x\to x_0} u(x)=+\infty$ for any $x_0\in\partial \Omega_1\setminus\partial\Omega$.
conclusions: There exists $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega)$ a weak solution of $(**)$
any weak solution satisfies $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ and $\lim_{x\to x_0} u(x)=+\infty$ for any $x_0\in\partial \Omega_1\setminus\partial\Omega$.
nodes.label: weak existence

nodes.name: Uniform integral estimate for $1/|\nabla u_\varepsilon|$
nodes.statement: Let $u_{{\varepsilon}}\in C^\infty(\Omega_0)$ be a solution of $(*_{{\varepsilon}})$ as in Theorem~\ref{blowup}. Then \begin{equation} \int_{\Omega_0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\nabla{u}_{\varepsilon}|^2}}dx\leq|\partial\Omega_0|+(n+2)\lambda|\Omega|, \end{equation} where $\lambda=\max_i\{|\lambda_i|, \lambda_i\text{ eigenvalue of } K\}$.
assumptions: Let $u_{{\varepsilon}}\in C^\infty(\Omega_0)$ be a solution of $(*_{{\varepsilon}})$ as in Theorem~\ref{blowup}.
nodes.label: normalintest

nodes.name: Integral estimate
nodes.statement: \int_{\Omega_0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\nabla{u}_{\varepsilon}|^2}}dx\leq|\partial\Omega_0|+(n+2)\lambda|\Omega|,
nodes.label: intest

nodes.name: Area of $\partial\Omega_0$ depends only on the data
nodes.statement: Note that $|\partial\Omega_0|=|\partial\Omega|+|\Sigma_\text{out}|$, where $\Sigma_\text{out}$ is the outermost MOTS. In \cite{AM09} an estimate, in terms of the initial data, on $|\Sigma_\infty|$ is derived and therefore $|\partial\Omega_0|$ depends only on the initial data and $\Omega$.
nodes.label: rmk on normalintest

nodes.name: Proof of the integral estimate
nodes.statement:
This follows as in \cite[Lemma 2.1]{MS}, keeping track of the extra ``$P$-term''. Let $\psi$ be a smooth function such that $0\leq\psi\leq1$, $\psi=1$ on $\Omega_{\delta}:=\{x\in\Omega_0|	ext{dist}(x,\partial\Omega_0)>\delta\}$, $\psi=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and $|D\psi|\leq\gamma/\delta$ for some $\gamma>1,\,\delta>0$. Multiplying $(*_{\varepsilon})$ by $\psi$ and integrating by parts we find  egin{equation*} egin{split} \int_{\Omega_\delta} rac{1 }{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|
abla u_{\varepsilon}|^2}}dx\leq \int_{\Omega_0\setminus\Omega_{\delta}} rac{
abla \psi\cdot 
abla u_{\varepsilon}}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|
abla u_{\varepsilon}|^2}}dx+\int_{\Omega_0}P(u_\varepsilon)\psi dx, \end{split}\end{equation*} where $P(u_\varepsilon)=\left(g^{ij}- rac{
abla^i u_\varepsilon
abla^j u_\varepsilon}{|
abla u_\varepsilon|^2+\varepsilon^2}ight) K_{ij}$. Since $|P(u_\varepsilon)|\le (n+2)\lambda$, we have \[\int_{\Omega_\delta} rac{1 }{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|
abla u_{\varepsilon}|^2}}dx\leq rac{\gamma}{\delta}|\Omega_0\setminus\Omega_{\delta}|+(n+2)\lambda|\Omega|\] and after letting $\delta	o 0$ and then $\gamma	o 1$ we obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply $(*_\varepsilon)$ by a cut-off and integrate by parts, bounding the $P$-term by $(n+2)\lambda$.

nodes.name: Follow Metzger-Schulze
nodes.statement: This follows as in \cite[Lemma 2.1]{MS}, keeping track of the extra ``$P$-term''.
nodes.statement_short: Adapt [MS, Lemma 2.1] tracking the $P$-term.

nodes.name: Integrate against a cut-off
nodes.statement:
Let $\psi$ be a smooth function such that $0\leq\psi\leq1$, $\psi=1$ on $\Omega_{\delta}:=\{x\in\Omega_0|	ext{dist}(x,\partial\Omega_0)>\delta\}$, $\psi=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and $|D\psi|\leq\gamma/\delta$ for some $\gamma>1,\,\delta>0$. Multiplying $(*_{\varepsilon})$ by $\psi$ and integrating by parts we find  egin{equation*} egin{split} \int_{\Omega_\delta} rac{1 }{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|
abla u_{\varepsilon}|^2}}dx\leq \int_{\Omega_0\setminus\Omega_{\delta}} rac{
abla \psi\cdot 
abla u_{\varepsilon}}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|
abla u_{\varepsilon}|^2}}dx+\int_{\Omega_0}P(u_\varepsilon)\psi dx, \end{split}\end{equation*} where $P(u_\varepsilon)=\left(g^{ij}- rac{
abla^i u_\varepsilon
abla^j u_\varepsilon}{|
abla u_\varepsilon|^2+\varepsilon^2}ight) K_{ij}$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by a cut-off $\psi$ and integrate by parts.

nodes.name: Bound and pass to limits
nodes.statement: Since $|P(u_\varepsilon)|\le (n+2)\lambda$, we have \[\int_{\Omega_\delta}\frac{1 }{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^2}}dx\leq\frac{\gamma}{\delta}|\Omega_0\setminus\Omega_{\delta}|+(n+2)\lambda|\Omega|\] and after letting $\delta\to 0$ and then $\gamma\to 1$ we obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|P|$ and let $\delta\to0$, $\gamma\to1$.

nodes.name: Strong convergence of normalized gradients
assumptions: Let $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1)$ be a weak solution of $(**)$
$\{u_{\varepsilon_k}\}$ be a sequence of solutions to the problems $(*_{\varepsilon_k})$ such that $ u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u$ in $C^0({\Omega_1}\cup\partial\Omega)$

$|

abla u
